title: API Rate Limiter
prompt: Our public API runs on about 150 gateway servers. Design the system that limits how many requests each API key, user or IP address can make, so one noisy customer cannot take the platform down.

clarify.q: What do we limit by: API key, signed-in user, IP address, endpoint, or a mix?
clarify.why: The limiter key decides the number of counters and whether we need identity before limiting. IP limits can run at the edge; per-key limits need the request authenticated first.

clarify.q: Are limits per plan, and do they change often?
clarify.why: If sales can change a customer's limit, rules must live in a config store and reach every gateway within seconds without a deploy.

clarify.q: Should short bursts be allowed, or is a hard 'N per minute' required?
clarify.why: Allowing bursts points to a token bucket. A strict count over a rolling window points to a sliding window. The two use different state and memory.

clarify.q: How exact must the limit be? Is 5% over acceptable?
clarify.why: Exactness costs a shared counter on every request. If small overshoot is fine, gateways can batch or reserve tokens locally and touch the shared store far less often.

clarify.q: What should happen if the limiter itself is unavailable: let traffic through or block it?
clarify.why: This is the main availability decision. Failing open risks overload, failing closed turns a limiter outage into an API outage, and the right answer differs per endpoint.

clarify.q: Is the limit global across regions or per region?
clarify.why: A truly global exact count needs a cross-region round trip of 70–150 ms per request. Per-region limits stay local and fast.

clarify.q: What peak request rate and how many gateway servers?
clarify.why: Sets how many shared-store operations per second we need and how wrong a purely local per-server limit would be.

functional: Enforce rules such as 1 000 requests/minute per API key with bursts up to 50, 60/minute per IP for anonymous calls, and 5/minute per user on login.
Rejected requests get HTTP 429 with Retry-After and remaining-quota headers; allowed requests carry the remaining quota too.
Operators can add or change a rule, or give one customer a temporary override, and it applies on all gateways within 10 seconds.
Each rule declares a failure mode (open or closed) used when the shared counter store is unavailable.
Every rejection is counted per rule and per key, so support can answer 'why was I blocked?'.
nonFunctional: Added latency per request: p50 under 0.5 ms, p99 under 2 ms.
Handles 500 000 requests/s at peak, growing to 5 M/s.
The limiter never makes the API less available than it would be without it: a store outage degrades limiting, not the API.
Accuracy: a key may exceed its limit by at most 5% under normal operation.
Rule changes propagate to all gateways in under 10 s.
outOfScope: Billing and monthly quotas (counted in a separate metering pipeline).
Volumetric DDoS protection at the network layer, which the CDN or cloud provider absorbs before traffic reaches us.

assumptions: 500 000 requests/s at peak across 150 gateway servers
Each request matches 2 rules on average (per key + per endpoint), checked in one Redis call
About 10 M distinct limiter keys active within an hour
One Redis shard sustains about 60 000 Lua script calls/s with headroom (one core per shard)

steps.label: Shared-store calls
steps.math: 500 000 req/s × 1 call (both rules in one script)

steps.label: Memory: token bucket
steps.math: 10 M keys × ~150 B (key + 2 fields + overhead) = 1.5 GB; / 10 shards

steps.label: Memory: sliding log
steps.math: 10 M keys × 50 timestamps in window × ~64 B = 32 GB; a key at 1 000/min holds 1 000 × 64 B = 64 KB
steps.result: ≈ 32 GB total, about 20× the bucket. Avoid for high limits

steps.label: Why not local-only counters
steps.math: 1 000/min per key spread over 150 gateways = 1 000 / 150 ≈ 6.7/min per gateway
steps.result: Per-gateway limits would be far too coarse for per-key rules; we need a shared count

estimates.takeaway:
The shared state is small: 1.5 GB of buckets. The real cost is operations per second, about 500 000 Redis calls at peak, so throughput sets the shard count, not memory. Ten shards handle it, and one call per request keeps added latency near one network round trip (about 0.5 ms inside an availability zone).

The sliding-log number shows why storing every timestamp is a bad default at these limits. The last line shows why each gateway cannot just count on its own. With 150 servers, a per-key limit split evenly is under 7 requests per minute per server, which is meaningless.

api.body: subject = apiKey | userId | ip; rules resolved from the request route and plan
api.note: An in-process library in the gateway, not a network service. It makes one Redis call that evaluates all matched rules atomically.

api.returns: 429 Too Many Requests · Retry-After: 12 · RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset
api.note: Allowed responses carry the same remaining-quota headers, so well-behaved clients slow down before hitting 429.

api.body: { match: { plan?, route?, method? }, keyBy, limit, periodSec, burst, cost?, failMode }
api.note: Admin only. Validated (no limit of 0 on wildcard routes), versioned, rolled out to 5% of gateways first.
Support can lift a customer's limit for a launch without changing their plan.
Lets customers see their own usage. Reads bucket state without consuming tokens.

entities.name: Rule
entities.store: Postgres (source of truth), cached in memory on every gateway
entities.why: A few hundred rows that change rarely. Gateways need them on every request, so they hold a full copy and refresh on a change notification, plus a full reload every 30 s.

entities.name: Bucket
entities.why: Two numbers per (subject, rule). The {subject} hash tag places all rules for one subject on the same shard, so one Lua script can check them together.

entities.name: Override
entities.why: Per-customer exceptions kept apart from plan rules, so they expire on their own and do not clutter the rule set.

data.note: Bucket state is disposable. Losing it only means some customers get a fresh bucket, so we keep it in memory only (no AOF) and replicate asynchronously for fast failover. Keys expire once a bucket would be full again, so idle keys cost nothing. Rules are the opposite: tiny, important and audited, so they live in Postgres with a history table.

hld.summary:
Limiting runs in three layers. The CDN/edge applies coarse per-IP limits to absorb floods cheaply. The API gateway authenticates the request, finds the matching rules in its in-memory copy, and calls the limiter library. The library runs one Lua script on the Redis shard that owns the subject. Allowed requests go to backend services, and rejected ones get a 429 straight from the gateway, so backends never see them.

A small Rules service stores rules in Postgres and publishes change events. Gateways subscribe and also poll every 30 s, in case they miss an event. Gateways emit allow and reject metrics per rule. Each gateway also keeps a local fallback limiter, used only while Redis is unhealthy.

diagram.title: Where the limiter sits
diagram.src:
flowchart LR

  E --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> G1["API gateway + limiter library"]
  LB --> G2["API gateway + limiter library"]

  G2 --> R

  RS -. change events .-> G2

flows.title: An allowed request
steps: Gateway authenticates the API key and matches 2 rules from its in-memory rule set.
Library checks its local deny cache. Nothing is cached for this key, so it calls EVALSHA on the shard for rl:{key}.
The script refills both buckets by elapsed time, finds tokens available in each, takes 1 from each, and writes them back.
Gateway forwards the request with the remaining-quota response headers. Total added time is about 0.5 ms.

flows.title: A rejected request
steps: The script finds the per-key bucket at 0.4 tokens and returns allowed = false, retryAfterMs = 36.
Gateway returns 429 with Retry-After and does not call the backend.
Gateway stores 'key denied until now + 36 ms' in its local deny cache, so a client hammering this gateway does not hit Redis again until then.
A reject counter for (ruleId, key) is incremented for dashboards and support.

flows.title: Changing a rule
steps: Operator PUTs a new limit. Rules service validates it, bumps the version and writes the row and an audit entry.
It publishes the change. 5% of gateways apply it first, and the rest apply it after 2 minutes if the reject rate looks normal.
Existing buckets keep their tokens. The new capacity and rate apply from the next check, because the script reads them as arguments.

deepDives.title: Choosing the algorithm
deepDives.problem: '1 000 requests per minute' sounds precise, but there are several ways to count it. They differ in burst behaviour, memory and how many Redis operations they need. The interviewer wants to hear the boundary problem and the memory cost, not just names.

options.name: Fixed window counter
options.how: INCR a counter for key:minute and reject when it passes the limit. The counter expires with the window.
pros: One INCR, about 50 bytes per key
Easy to explain to customers
cons: Bursts at the boundary: 1 000 requests at 0:59 and 1 000 more at 1:00 allows 2 000 in two seconds, double the intended rate
Everyone's window resets at the same instant, so traffic spikes at the start of each minute

options.name: Sliding log
options.how: Store a timestamp for every request in a sorted set. Remove those older than 60 s, then count what remains.
pros: Exact over any rolling 60 s
Easy to reason about
cons: Memory grows with the limit: 64 KB for a key at 1 000/min, ≈ 32 GB across our 10 M keys
Rejected requests must still be cleaned up, and the work per call grows with traffic

options.name: Sliding window counter
options.how: Keep counts for the current and previous fixed window and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps. Example: limit 100, previous minute 80, current 30, 15 s into the minute: 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90, so allow.
pros: Two integers per key, so tiny memory
Smooths the boundary burst, and the error is small when traffic is fairly even
cons: An approximation: it assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly
No explicit burst setting, so 'allow 50 at once, then 1 000/min' cannot be expressed

options.name: Token bucket
options.how: A bucket holds up to burst tokens and refills at limit/period. Each request takes cost tokens. State is (tokens, lastRefill). Refill happens lazily on each check: tokens = min(burst, tokens + elapsed × rate).
pros: Separates sustained rate (16.7/s) from burst size (50), which is what API customers actually need
Two numbers per key and O(1) per check
Weighted cost is natural: an export call can cost 20 tokens
cons: Harder for customers to reason about than 'N per minute'
Needs a clock for refill, so clock disagreements between callers matter (see race conditions)

deepDives.choice:
Token bucket for per-key and per-user API rules, because plans are sold as a sustained rate plus a burst, and costs per endpoint fall out naturally. Sliding window counter for simple per-IP rules at the edge, where 'about 60 per minute' is good enough and state must be minimal.

What would change my mind: a contract that promises 'never more than N in any 60-second span', for example a downstream partner's hard limit. That needs an exact sliding log, and only for that one low-volume rule.

deepDives.title: Counting across 150 gateways
deepDives.problem: A customer's requests land on any gateway. Each gateway alone sees about 1/150 of the traffic, so the count must be shared. But a network call per request adds latency and creates a dependency on the shared store.

options.name: Central store on every request
options.how: Every check is an atomic script on the Redis shard that owns the key.
pros: Accurate to the request
Gateways stay stateless
Simple mental model
cons: One network round trip per request (about 0.3–0.5 ms in-zone)
Redis becomes a hard dependency that needs a failure plan
One very hot key loads one shard

options.name: Local counters, synced periodically
options.how: Each gateway counts locally and every 100–500 ms pushes its deltas to a shared store and pulls the global totals. It decides locally from the last known total.
pros: No network call on the request path
Shared-store load drops from 500 000/s to about 150 gateways × 10 syncs/s = 1 500 calls/s
cons: Overshoot: within one sync interval every gateway can admit a full burst, up to 150× the burst in the worst case
More complex merging logic, harder to test

options.name: Central store with local token leasing
options.how: For high-volume keys, a gateway takes a lease of k tokens (say 10) in one Redis call and spends them locally. Unused tokens expire with the lease.
pros: Redis calls fall by about k× for heavy keys
Overshoot is bounded: at most k tokens per gateway
cons: Low-volume keys gain nothing and can be under-served if leases sit idle on other gateways
Another tuning knob per rule

options.name: Sticky routing by key
options.how: The load balancer hashes the API key to a gateway, so one gateway sees all of a key's traffic and counts it in memory.
pros: No shared store at all
Exact and fast
cons: Uneven load: one huge customer pins one gateway
Every gateway restart or scale event moves keys, and their counts start over
IP and key limits need different routing, which cannot both be sticky

deepDives.choice:
Central Redis on every request, plus a local deny cache. At 500 000 calls/s, ten shards are cheap and the 5% accuracy target rules out periodic sync, which can overshoot badly. The deny cache means an abusive client sending 100 000 req/s mostly hits gateway memory, not Redis.

What would change my mind: at 10× traffic (5 M/s) I would add token leasing for keys above about 100 req/s. That cuts Redis calls roughly tenfold for the heaviest keys while keeping overshoot to 10 tokens per gateway.

deepDives.title: Race conditions and clocks
deepDives.problem: Two gateways check the same key at the same moment. If each reads tokens = 1, decides 'allow', and writes tokens = 0, both requests pass. That is a classic lost update. Under load, a burst of 50 can become 50 × the number of concurrent readers. Clocks are a second issue: gateways compute refill from elapsed time, and their clocks disagree by milliseconds.

options.name: Read, decide, write from the gateway
options.how: HMGET the bucket, compute in the gateway, then HMSET.
pros: Simple code
cons: Lost updates under concurrency, so limits leak exactly when traffic is heavy
Two round trips

options.name: Optimistic transaction (WATCH / MULTI)
options.how: WATCH the key, read, compute, and EXEC the write. Retry if another client changed the key in between.
pros: Correct
Logic stays in the gateway language
cons: Hot keys cause retry storms, exactly when the limiter matters most
Two or more round trips

options.name: Atomic server-side script
options.how: A Lua script reads the bucket, refills, decides, writes and sets the TTL in one step. Redis runs scripts one at a time per shard, so there is no interleaving. The script reads the time from the Redis server, so all gateways share one clock per key.
pros: One round trip, no lost updates
One clock per key removes skew between gateways
Can check several rules for the same subject atomically when the keys share a hash tag
cons: Scripts block the shard while running, so they must stay tiny (microseconds)
Script code needs versioning and loading (SCRIPT LOAD / EVALSHA)

deepDives.choice:
Atomic Lua script with the Redis server time. In plain words: now = TIME; tokens = min(burst, tokens + (now − ts) × rate); if tokens ≥ cost then tokens −= cost, allowed; save tokens, ts = now; PEXPIRE key ttl, then return allowed, remaining and the retry time (cost − tokens) / rate. If the time ever goes backwards after a failover, the script treats elapsed as 0 instead of a negative refill.

With fixed windows a plain INCR is already atomic. The trap there is INCR followed by a separate EXPIRE: if the gateway dies between them, the key never expires and the customer is locked out forever. Use one script, or SET key 0 EX 60 NX before INCR.

What would change my mind: a store without scripting, such as a managed key-value store. Then I would use its conditional write (compare-and-set on a version), and accept retries on hot keys.

diagram.title: Two gateways race for the last token
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant G1 as Gateway 1
  participant G2 as Gateway 2
  participant R as Redis shard
  G1->>R: EVALSHA bucket for key A
  G2->>R: EVALSHA bucket for key A
  Note over R: scripts run one at a time
  R-->>G1: allowed, remaining 0
  R-->>G2: rejected, retry after 60 ms
  G1->>G1: forward to backend
  G2->>G2: return 429 and cache the deny

deepDives.title: Where the limiter lives
deepDives.problem: Limits can be enforced in the client, at the CDN edge, at the gateway, in a sidecar, or inside each service. Each place sees different information and has a different cost per rejected request.

options.name: Edge or CDN
options.how: Per-IP rules in the CDN or a web application firewall in front of everything.
pros: Rejects floods before they cost us anything
Scales with the provider
cons: Knows only the IP and URL, not the API key or plan
Carrier NAT puts thousands of mobile users behind one IP, so per-IP limits must stay loose

options.name: API gateway
options.how: After authentication, the gateway applies per-key, per-user and per-route rules using the shared store.
pros: Has identity and plan, which most rules need
One place to configure, and backends never see rejected traffic
cons: Cannot see business facts, such as 'SMS sent to this phone number today'
The gateway team owns everyone's rules

options.name: Inside the service
options.how: The service calls the same limiter library with its own keys, for example otp:{phone}.
pros: Can limit by domain facts the gateway never sees
Owned by the team that understands the cost
cons: Work has already been spent getting the request this far
Risk of each team building its own limiter, so share one library

deepDives.choice:
All three, each doing one job. The edge drops IP floods with loose limits. The gateway owns plan quotas, the rules customers see in headers. Services use the shared library for business limits like OTP sends per phone number, which is also where we protect money, since SMS costs real cash.

What would change my mind: an internal-only API with a few trusted callers. Then a gateway layer alone, or even per-service concurrency limits, is enough.

deepDives.title: When Redis is down
deepDives.problem: The limiter is on every request. If a Redis shard is slow or gone, we must decide in milliseconds whether to let traffic through. Waiting on a dead Redis turns a limiter problem into a full API outage.

options.name: Fail open
options.how: On timeout or error, allow the request and log it.
pros: The API stays up
Correct for most endpoints, since limits protect capacity that usually has some headroom
cons: During the outage, abusive clients are unlimited
Expensive endpoints, such as SMS or login, can be abused for cost or brute force

options.name: Fail closed
pros: Safe for endpoints where abuse is costly or dangerous
cons: A cache outage becomes an API outage for every customer

options.name: Fall back to local limiting
options.how: A circuit breaker opens after 50% errors over 5 s (call timeout 5 ms). While open, each gateway enforces a local token bucket at limit × 1.5 / 150 per gateway, then probes Redis every 10 s.
pros: Still stops the worst abuse
No extra infrastructure
cons: Inaccurate: a key whose traffic lands on few gateways gets less than its limit, and one spread evenly gets about 1.5×
Local state must be bounded (an LRU of 100 000 keys)

deepDives.choice:
Per-rule failure mode, defaulting to local fallback. General API rules fall back to local buckets, generous enough that real customers rarely notice. Login, password reset and OTP rules are marked failMode: closed, and they fall back to strict local limits, because brute force and SMS cost matter more than convenience there. The 5 ms timeout and circuit breaker mean a dead shard costs at most 5 ms on a handful of requests before the breaker opens.

One shard failing affects only the keys on that shard. Replicas are promoted in a few seconds, and losing a few seconds of bucket state just gives some customers a full bucket, which is harmless.

What would change my mind: if the limiter protects a fragile backend that falls over at 1.2× load, failing open is not an option, and I would put load shedding (concurrency limits) in the backend itself.

failures: Replica promoted in a few seconds. Gateways use local fallback for that shard while the breaker is open. Buckets on the replica may be a few ms stale, which slightly over-allows: accepted.
A bad rule (limit 0 on /*) is pushed

Validation rejects zero limits on wildcard routes, rollout goes to 5% of gateways first with automatic rollback if 429s jump above 3× baseline, and every rule has a one-click revert to the previous version.
Clients retry immediately after 429, multiplying load
Retry-After on every 429, official SDKs back off exponentially with jitter, and the local deny cache answers repeat offenders without touching Redis.
One abusive key sends 200 000 req/s, all on one Redis shard
The local deny cache absorbs repeats until the retry time. If it continues, auto-block the key at the edge for 10 minutes and page on-call.
Gateways disagree on time by 50 ms
Not an issue for correctness, because the script uses the Redis server time. Gateway time is only used for the local deny cache, where small skew is harmless.
A slow Redis (not down) adds 20 ms to every request
Hard 5 ms timeout on limiter calls. Breaker opens on timeouts too, not just errors. Alert on limiter p99 above 2 ms.
scale: 10× (5 M req/s): 100 shards is possible but wasteful. Add token leasing for keys above about 100 req/s and send a fixed share of checks for low-risk rules through local-only buckets. Keep one round trip per request at most.

Multiple regions: give each region its own Redis and split a customer's global limit across regions by recent traffic share, rebalanced every minute. A cross-region check at 70–150 ms per request is never worth it.
Many more rule types: move rule matching to a compiled lookup (route trie + plan map), so matching stays under 10 µs with thousands of rules.

followups.q: A customer with a global limit sends traffic from three regions. How do you keep the total right?
answer: Run limiting per region against local Redis and give each region a share of the limit, for example 60/30/10 based on the last 5 minutes of traffic.
A background job recomputes the shares every minute from per-region usage, so a customer moving traffic between regions is rebalanced quickly.
Accept a few percent of error during shifts. Exact global limits need cross-region coordination on every request, which costs more than the error.

followups.q: Some requests are much more expensive than others. How do you limit fairly?
answer: Give each route a cost in tokens: a simple read costs 1, a search 5, an export 50.
For GraphQL, compute a cost from the query's depth and list sizes before running it, and charge that.
Optionally reconcile after the request using real CPU time, charging the difference to a second 'compute' bucket.

followups.q: What is the difference between rate limiting and concurrency limiting, and when do you need the second?
answer: A rate limit caps requests per unit of time. A concurrency limit caps requests in flight at once.
Slow endpoints (reports, uploads) can exhaust workers at a low request rate, so they need an in-flight cap per customer.
Implement it as a counter incremented on start and decremented on finish, with a lease expiry so crashed requests release their slot.

followups.q: How do you test that the limiter really holds 1 000/min under concurrency?
answer: A load test with 200 concurrent clients on one key across many gateways. Assert the accepted count per minute stays within 5% of the limit.
Fault injection: kill a Redis primary mid-test and check that the fallback kicks in within 5 s and the API error rate stays flat.
A property test of the script logic: random sequences of time and cost never let tokens go above burst or below zero.

followups.q: Mobile users behind carrier NAT share one IP. How do you avoid blocking them?
answer: Keep per-IP limits loose (they are a flood guard) and put real limits on identity: API key, user or device token.
For anonymous endpoints, issue a signed anonymous token on first contact and limit by that token.
Allow-list known carrier NAT ranges at higher limits, and watch false-positive reports.

mistakes: Read-then-write from the gateway without atomicity, so the limit leaks under exactly the concurrency it is meant to control.
Never saying what happens when Redis is down, or answering 'fail closed' for everything.
Choosing fixed windows without mentioning the 2× boundary burst.
Storing a timestamp per request (sliding log) for 10 M keys without doing the memory maths.
Putting the limiter in a separate network service, adding a second hop, when a library plus Redis gives the same result in one hop.

mid: Asked what the limit key is (API key, user, IP) and whether bursts are allowed
Named at least two algorithms and explained the fixed-window boundary burst with numbers
Placed the limiter in the gateway after authentication and returned 429 with Retry-After
Used a shared store so limits hold across all gateways, and sized it from requests per second
Made the check atomic (script or INCR), not read-then-write
senior: Chose an algorithm per rule type and justified it (token bucket for plans, sliding window for IPs)
Gave a concrete Redis-down plan: timeout, circuit breaker, fail open vs closed per rule
Handled hot or abusive keys without overloading one shard (local deny cache)
Used server-side time or explained how gateway clock skew affects refill
Described rule rollout without deploys, including a guard against a bad rule
staff: Discussed global limits across regions and chose per-region shares over cross-region checks
Introduced token leasing or batching with a stated overshoot bound when traffic grows 10×
Separated rate limits from concurrency limits and load shedding, and said when each is the right tool
Defined how to measure limiter accuracy and false positives in production
